sources.title: Actualización de la Contribución Determinada a nivel Nacional 3.0 de México
sources.organization: Secretaría de Medio Ambiente y Recursos Naturales (SEMARNAT), Government of Mexico; submitted to UNFCCC
sources.temporal_coverage: NDC 3.0 published in 2025; reports current and historical conditions and sets proposed actions through 2035.
sources.methodology: Government NDC synthesizes national diagnostics and proposed climate measures.
sources.limitations: Costa Chica annex is regional; proposed measures are not evaluated outcomes.

sources.title: Panorama nacional de datos, tendencias y respuestas políticas al nexo entre migración, medio ambiente y cambio climático (MMACC) en México
sources.temporal_coverage: Published 2025; reviews migration, disaster and climate evidence, including relocations through November 2024 and earlier cases.
sources.methodology: IOM synthesis of scientific literature, policy, programmes, laws and documented mobility cases.
sources.limitations: Evidence is stronger in central-southern Mexico; the report notes research gaps in the north.

sources.title: Mexico Poverty and Equity Assessment
sources.temporal_coverage: Published 2024; climate exposure estimates mainly use 2020 population and poverty-vulnerability estimates use data through 2022.
sources.methodology: World Bank analysis combines census, household-survey, hazard-exposure and poverty-risk measures.
sources.limitations: State vulnerability rates are estimates cited from a separate ENIGH-based model, not conflict measures.

sources.title: Climate Change and Migration from Central America: Insights from Migrants in Mexico
sources.organization: University of California, Berkeley School of Law Human Rights Clinic, in partnership with the Institute for Women in Migration (IMUMI)
sources.temporal_coverage: Published April 2026; survey and interviews concern migrants in Mexico during July-December 2024.
sources.methodology: Report combines a 2024 survey of 87 migrants in transit, key-informant interviews and desk research.
sources.limitations: Small, non-representative sample; security findings principally concern migrants from four Central American countries.

sources.title: Norma Oficial Mexicana NOM-003-SEDATU-2023: Lineamientos para el fortalecimiento del sistema territorial ante amenazas naturales y cambio climático
sources.organization: Secretaría de Desarrollo Agrario, Territorial y Urbano (SEDATU), Government of Mexico; Diario Oficial de la Federación
geographic_coverage: regional, state, metropolitan and municipal planning scales
sources.temporal_coverage: Published 14 February 2024; applies to preparation or updating of territorial and urban-development plans.
sources.methodology: Official standard sets national multiscale territorial-planning guidelines.
sources.limitations: Normative requirements; the standard does not report implementation or compliance results.

claims.locator: PDF physical p.20 (printed p.20), national context.
claims.paraphrase: NDC 3.0 reports intensifying extreme hydrometeorological events, altered rainfall, rising temperatures and seas, and pressure on water availability.
claims.limitations: National summary, not a district risk estimate.

claims.locator: PDF physical p.149 (printed p.149), priority-populations annex.
claims.paraphrase: Mostly in Guerrero and Oaxaca’s Costa Chica, 16 municipalities have over 40% Afro-Mexican residents; coastal zones face floods, heat, salinity, sea rise and erosion.
claims.limitations: NDC gives regional concentration, not municipality-specific hazard rates.

claims.locator: PDF physical pp.87-88 (printed pp.87-88), adaptation axis F.
claims.paraphrase: NDC frames climate risks as threats to social cohesion and peace through crises, population displacement and conflict escalation.
claims.limitations: Government policy diagnosis, not a local conflict-incidence estimate.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: NDC states climate change exacerbates existing conflicts and could destabilize regions.

claims.locator: PDF physical pp.88-89 (printed pp.88-89) and pp.152-153 (printed pp.152-153).
claims.paraphrase: NDC says environmental offenses may obstruct climate action and environmental defenders face homicide, intimidation and criminalization.
claims.limitations: National description; proposed prevention and mediation measures are not evaluated outcomes.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: It links environmental crimes to obstruction of climate action and proposes conflict-sensitive adaptation and community mediation.

claims.locator: PDF physical p.7 (printed p.4), summary messages on socioeconomic conditions and mobility.
claims.paraphrase: IOM identifies inequality, poverty, weak disaster assistance, limited credit and inadequate services as barriers to local resilience, especially for women and marginalized groups.
claims.limitations: National synthesis; conditions and effects vary by region.

claims.locator: PDF physical p.8 (printed p.5), planned-relocation summary.
claims.paraphrase: IOM documents post-1998 relocations in Motozintla, Frontera-Comalapa, Huixtla and Comitán, and post-Hurricane Stan relocations in Chiapas.
claims.limitations: Cases date from 1998 and 2005; the synthesis does not evaluate long-term outcomes.

claims.locator: PDF physical p.8 (printed p.5), El Bosque relocation summary.
claims.paraphrase: IOM reports 51 families from El Bosque, Centla, were relocated to Frontera in November 2024 after reporting sea-level effects since 2019.
claims.limitations: Report gives relocation count and reported trigger, not subsequent outcomes.

claims.locator: PDF physical p.7 (printed p.4), socioenvironmental conflict and displacement summary.
claims.paraphrase: IOM cites over 600 megaprojects since 2017; at least half involved social or ecological conflict, and some land- or water-use projects may displace people.
claims.limitations: IOM does not attribute these project conflicts or displacement cases to climate change.

claims.locator: PDF physical p.59 (printed p.59), section 3, climate-event poverty vulnerability.
claims.paraphrase: A cited 2022 model estimates climate-shock poverty vulnerability above 60% in Chiapas, Oaxaca and Guerrero, versus below 15% in several northern states.
affected_groups: households at risk of falling into poverty
claims.limitations: Assessment cites a separate ENIGH-based model and an explicit poverty-fall threshold.

claims.locator: PDF physical p.55 (printed p.55), map discussion of state exposure.
claims.paraphrase: WB maps place high drought exposure in Chihuahua, Durango, Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí; flood exposure clusters in Tabasco and Guerrero-Michoacán coasts.
claims.limitations: Map thresholds define extreme events; exposure does not alone measure impact or capacity.

claims.locator: PDF physical p.58 (printed p.58), table 3 and discussion.
claims.paraphrase: Poor residents are more exposed than non-poor to drought and landslides; the assessment relates drought exposure to rural and agricultural livelihoods.
claims.limitations: Population exposure estimates are based on the report's reference-year census and hazard thresholds.

claims.locator: PDF physical p.62 (printed p.62), transport access and territorial context.
claims.paraphrase: Low paved-road and transport access localities cluster in the sierras of Guerrero, Oaxaca and Chiapas, where transport is key to reaching services.
claims.limitations: Road-access finding is not a direct measure of disaster-response performance.

claims.locator: PDF physical pp.6-7 (printed pp.II-III), executive summary; methodology p.13.
claims.paraphrase: In the 2024 transit survey, 66% cited insecurity and 62% violence; climate shocks sometimes deepened precarity and exposure to harm.
claims.limitations: 87 respondents; small non-representative sample, with climate and violence largely in origin countries.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: Report says climate shocks can compound insecurity and increase exposure to violence or exploitation.

claims.locator: PDF physical pp.6-7 (printed pp.II-III), executive summary survey results.
claims.paraphrase: Women respondents more often reported work, food and water disruption after climate events; 22% of female respondents said they fled gender-based violence.
claims.limitations: Small non-representative sample; the report does not attribute all violence to climate events.

claims.locator: PDF physical pp.7-8 (printed pp.III-IV), protection-system findings.
claims.paraphrase: Report identifies detention-focused migration enforcement, under-resourced COMAR and rarely granted disaster visas as barriers in Mexico's protection system.
claims.limitations: Study assesses access and policy as of its 2024 research period; not an administrative audit.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: Report says these constraints limit physical and legal access to protection for climate-affected migrants.

claims.locator: Official text lines 146-153 and 283-295; sections 1.1, 1.2 and 4.1.1.
claims.paraphrase: NOM-003 requires regional, state, metropolitan and municipal plans to integrate risk instruments and climate measures into territorial planning.
claims.limitations: Normative requirement; the standard does not measure compliance.

claims.locator: Official text lines 494-496, municipal social lineamientos.
claims.paraphrase: Municipal guidelines call for neighborhood and locality networks with authorities and civil protection for prevention, response and resilient recovery.
claims.limitations: Guideline, not evidence that networks have been established or tested.

search_audit.query: Mexico subnational climate vulnerability poverty Chiapas Guerrero Oaxaca report drought flood World Bank
search_audit.outcome: Read World Bank state-level exposure and poverty-risk estimates, NDC Costa Chica annex and IOM's named Tabasco and Chiapas relocation cases.

search_audit.query: Mexico climate change security social cohesion conflict socioenvironmental climate NDC environmental defenders
search_audit.outcome: NDC directly frames climate risks as conflict and cohesion concerns; Berkeley survey evidence concerns Central American migrants transiting Mexico, not Mexico-origin households.

search_audit.query: Mexico insecurity violence disrupt climate adaptation project delivery environmental defenders climate resilience
search_audit.outcome: NDC says environmental offenses can obstruct climate action and proposes prevention and mediation; no directly read source documents insecurity halting a named adaptation project.

search_audit.query: Mexico local climate adaptation resilience community implementation official report water monitoring relocation
search_audit.outcome: Read SEDATU's operative planning standard and IOM's documented relocations; NDC measures are recorded as proposals, not evaluated capacity.

gaps: The official CONAPO/UNHCR 2026 diagnosis on climate- and disaster-related internal displacement could not be opened; its search-result description was not used as evidence.
The UNHCR Sin escape report PDF exceeded the web reader limit and was not used.
The UNFCCC registry listed a 2026-08 NDC attachment that timed out; claims cite only the directly inspected 2025-11 NDC 3.0 PDF.
The NDC's climate-security statements are a national policy diagnosis; the inspected sources do not measure local conflict incidence caused by climate change.

No directly read source established that armed insecurity interrupted delivery of a named Mexican climate-adaptation project; the NDC identifies environmental offenses as a risk to climate action and proposes prevention and mediation.
Berkeley/IMUMI's survey covers 87 Central American migrants in transit in Mexico and is non-representative; findings on climate and violence are not generalized to Mexico-origin communities.
IOM records relocations but does not assess their long-term livelihood, safety or social-cohesion outcomes; the 1998 and 2005 Chiapas cases are historical.
